summary_html: Findings by **federal/state oversight** (CFSR reviews, OIG audits, child-fatality commissions) can initiate investigations or corrective actions that open CPS involvement.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — national commission on child abuse/neglect fatalities  
- **Child & Family Services Reviews (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of state systems  
- **Inspector General Act (5 U.S.C. App.)** — OIG oversight of HHS/ACF and grantees

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Arkansas Department of Health v. Westark Christian Action Council
key_cases.holding: The court reversed, holding the requested reports were exempt vital records, while reaffirming that the FOIA is construed liberally toward disclosure and its exemptions are construed narrowly.
key_cases.relevance: It is the canonical Arkansas statement of the interpretive presumption that governs any records request used to trigger or document oversight.
key_cases.quote: we narrowly construe exceptions to the FOIA to counterbalance the self-protective instincts of the government bureaucracy

key_cases.case_name: Pulaski County v. Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, Inc.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the dispositive question was whether the withheld communications were 'public records' under the FOIA and that an in camera review was necessary to decide it, rather than a categorical exemption for personal material.
key_cases.relevance: It establishes the procedure a court uses when an agency claims withheld material is not a public record at all.
key_cases.quote: It is necessary to conduct an in camera review to determine whether the e-mails at issue are public records, and thus should be disclosed pursuant to the FOIA.

key_cases.case_name: Arkansas Department of Human Services v. Cole
key_cases.holding: The court struck down Initiated Act 1, which barred cohabiting unmarried adults from adopting or fostering, holding that conditioning the privilege of fostering or adopting on surrendering the state constitutional right to private consensual conduct is unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: It shows the Arkansas Constitution operating as an independent oversight constraint on statewide child-welfare placement policy.
key_cases.quote: We affirm the circuit court's ruling that Act 1 is unconstitutional as a violation of fundamental privacy rights under the Arkansas Constitution.

key_cases.case_name: Arkansas Department of Human Services v. Howard
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the invalidation of the Child Welfare Agency Review Board regulation barring any household with a homosexual adult from fostering, holding the rule had no rational relationship to child welfare and was an unauthorized exercise of legislative power over morality.
key_cases.relevance: It is the model for how a categorical agency placement rule is tested against the record and the agency's delegated authority when oversight bodies review it.
key_cases.quote: the circuit court did not err in finding that there was no rational relationship between the regulation's blanket exclusion and the health, safety, and welfare of the foster children

reporting_details: Arkansas is not a universal-reporting state: Ark. Code Ann. § 12-18-402(b) names 43 categories of mandated reporter — ending with any person 18 or older who observes abuse, sexual abuse, or sexual exploitation of a child — and § 12-18-402(a) requires each of them to notify the statewide Child Abuse Hotline immediately; mandated reporters may instead file through the secure portal at mandatedreporter.arkansas.gov, while everyone else calls the hotline. The hotline is answered by a civilian member of the Arkansas State Police Crimes Against Children Division (CACD), who decides whether a report is accepted; an accepted report is sent for investigation to either DCFS or CACD depending on the severity of the concerns reported, and Ark. Code Ann. § 12-18-602(a) places the investigation duty on both "[t]he Department of Human Services and the Division of Arkansas State Police."

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours (severe maltreatment, the neglect defined in § 12-18-103(14)(B), or a child's sudden and unexpected death); 72 hours for all other reports
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Initial notification of suspected child maltreatment received
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Ark. Code Ann. § 12-18-602

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days to make the investigative determination; one 15-day extension permitted (60 days maximum)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the child maltreatment report from the Child Abuse Hotline (9 CAR § 40-324(a))
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Ark. Code Ann. § 12-18-616(a)(2): the timing requirement "shall not be considered as a factor to alter the investigative determination in any judicial or administrative proceeding"
